Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Tane was 24 years old when the helicopter took fire. He remembers the exact moment—6:47 in the morning, the sun just beginning to break through the haze over the jungle canopy. The first round hit the fuselage and he was thrown sideways, his hand slamming against the shredded fabric of his seat, the coarse threads digging into his palm as he scrambled to brace himself. The sound of the rotors faltered, then screamed, then fell silent. He does not recall the crash itself, only the terror that arrived before impact and the texture of that seat fabric, which he can still feel against his skin if he lets himself think about it. For decades after, he told himself the memory belonged to someone else—a younger man, a different life. But the terror that accompanies recall is unmistakably his own, and it comes without warning. He will be standing in his kitchen or walking through an airport terminal and something in his surroundings—a rough fabric on a chair, the particular quality of early morning light, or the distant thrum of helicopter blades—brings the full memory crashing back, and he is back in that seat, waiting to die.

Tane returned home from the war and resumed his career as an airline pilot, a job he had loved since childhood. In the cockpit he was competent, focused, in control. But outside it, the world had become a different place. He noticed it first in small ways: rising before dawn to prepare for a flight, he would find himself checking the locks on the front door twice, then three times, unable to shake the feeling that something was waiting for him in the dark. He began to dread the night shift rotations, not because of the flying but because of the hours before and after, when the house was quiet and his wife slept and he lay awake, straining to hear sounds that did not belong. He came to believe that he was not safe at night, that darkness carried a threat he could not name. During the day, in public spaces, he found himself scanning every room he entered for the exits—mapping the doors, the windows, the emergency routes before he could pay attention to anything else. If someone moved suddenly beside him at the grocery store or in the airport lounge, his body would lock into a posture of readiness before his mind caught up. He knew it was irrational, but the feeling was undeniable: the world was a dangerous place, and he was the only one who seemed to see it.

The texture trigger was the hardest to escape. The seat fabric in his commercial aircraft was smooth, synthetic, nothing like the shredded canvas of the helicopter. But every time he ran his hand over the armrest during preflight checks, he had to suppress the urge to pull his hand back. He had learned to avoid touching certain materials altogether—rough wool blankets, coarse upholstery, the bristled surface of a new carpet. At home, his wife noticed that he had replaced all the throw pillows and refused to sit on the sofa if the fabric was textured. He told her it was a preference, but the truth was more complicated. He could not explain that the feel of a particular weave transported him to a moment of such terror that his heart would race and his palms would sweat, and he would have to excuse himself to the bathroom to breathe.

Over the years, the avoidance hardened into habit. He stopped flying early morning routes whenever possible, trading shifts with younger pilots to avoid the hour that had fractured his life. He told himself it was about the light, the glare, but really it was about the feeling of that 6:47 sky. He stopped attending gatherings where helicopters might be discussed or, worse, seen. He stopped watching films with combat scenes. He stopped talking about the war at all. Yet the memory did not stop arriving. It came unbidden, sometimes daily, and with it the certainty that something fundamental was wrong with him. He used to be a happy man—his wife reminded him of that, showed him old photos, described the way he used to laugh. But he could no longer access that person. He felt broken, defective, as though the man who survived the crash had not returned home but had been replaced by someone hollowed out and wary.

His marriage suffered. His wife grew tired of his silences, his hypervigilance, the way he would startle at her touch at night. She accused him of living in the past. He could not argue with her, because it was true, but he also could not stop. The memory felt alien—like a story he had been told about someone else—yet the terror it produced was immediate and physical, a betrayal of his own body. He had come to believe that he was beyond repair. The world was dangerous, and he was proof of it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of near-collapse in the cockpit. During a routine descent, the air traffic controller gave a sudden frequency change over the radio, and the unexpected shift in his headset—a crackle of static, a clipped tone—flooded him with the same warning sensation he had felt in the helicopter just before the rounds hit. His hands trembled on the controls. For a few seconds, he was not sure where he was. He landed safely, but the fright stayed with him. He told his wife that night, and she said nothing, but she held his hand. The next morning, he made the call. He is not sure what he is hoping for—only that he cannot keep living this way, haunted by a memory that does not feel like his own, in a world that does not feel safe, carrying a terror he cannot explain.
